title: Teaching Engineers, Trusting AI: How Education Enabled Autonomous Code Review
gist: Duolingo software engineer Sarah Deitke describes how a dedicated DevEx AI team drove AI tool adoption in a 300-person engineering org from 80% to 100% through workshops, observability dashboards and office hours, then used that trust to ship an LLM-based PR risk-assessment bot that auto-approves low-risk pull requests without human review. As auto-approved merges climbed from 0% to about 10% of all PRs over six months, median time to merge fell from roughly 18 hours to 12 hours with no discernible increase in defect rate.

themes.theme: AI adoption as culture, not tooling

insights.claim: Duolingo runs a dedicated DevEx AI team whose remit is enabling engineers to use AI effectively in their workflows — distinct from the traditional developer-experience team that owns merge queues and CI/CD.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: A separate AI-enablement function is emerging as an org-design pattern; most companies have tool access but no team owning adoption, which is where the value gap sits.
insights.quote: We're focused on how do we enable our engineers to use AI effectively in their workflows.
insights.locator: Sarah Deitke: I'm a software engineer at Duolingo

insights.claim: The blockers to AI adoption are identified as human rather than technical: engineer skepticism, core systems like code review being treated as sacred, unresolved accountability when one reviewer is an AI, and trust that is slow to build and fast to lose.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: If adoption is gated on trust rather than capability, model improvements alone will not convert into measured productivity — the bottleneck is organizational.
insights.quote: AI also challenges and changes accountability. This is a conversation my team has a lot.
insights.locator: AI Adoption is a Culture Change

insights.claim: AI-driven code generation has moved the delivery bottleneck from writing code to reviewing it, because PRs are now cheap to produce while human review capacity is unchanged.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: Identifies the next constraint in AI-assisted delivery — review and verification tooling is the category that must scale next.
insights.quote: it's easier to make PRs now, and so we see the bottleneck shifting to code review for shipping quickly
insights.locator: Case Study: Redesigning Code Review for Autonomous Systems

insights.claim: Duolingo reached 100% AI tool usage adoption among its engineers over the past year, up from 80% previously, which the speaker attributes to the education programme rather than to tool availability.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: A concrete adoption ceiling datapoint for AI coding tools in a motivated org — the last 20% required investment, not procurement.
insights.quote: we've hit the tail end of getting to 100% AI tool usage adoption for the engineers in our organization. Before that, it had been 80%
insights.locator: What are the results from Duolingo investing in so much AI education

insights.claim: Structured lab-style workshops on MCP servers, Cursor rules, LLM request batching and evaluations scored 95% of the engineering org reporting they learned something new and would recommend the format.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: Quantifies that internal enablement content works — and where enterprise AI training budget should go relative to tool licences.
insights.quote: 95% of our engineering org reported learning something new and that they would recommend this style training
insights.locator: Building AI Literacy Through Education

insights.claim: Engineers trust pre-vetted content produced by their own engineering organization considerably more than generic vendor-delivered training.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: A structural headwind for third-party AI training vendors selling into engineering orgs; internal enablement teams capture the value instead.
insights.quote: engineers trust the pre-vetted content from their engineering orgs a lot more than, say, bringing in a vendor and doing a more generic solution
insights.locator: Building AI Literacy Through Education

insights.claim: Duolingo built AI observability dashboards tracking daily active users by vendor, by business function, by developer community, and by IDE, programming language, token usage, cost and model family — and the dashboard itself started as and remains a vibe-coded project extended by prompting.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: Token, cost and model-family telemetry per function is the data leadership uses to justify AI spend; vendors that hide it lose the internal argument.
insights.quote: We could just go to our AI tools dashboard and say, ok, add me a chart that looks at this now.
insights.locator: building AI observability dashboards

insights.claim: AI support demand is spilling beyond engineering: Duolingo's 15-minute office hours are used heavily by adjacent roles such as learning designers needing GitHub to vibe-code projects and QA support staff scaling AI workflows off their own machines.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: The addressable user base for developer AI tools is expanding into non-engineering functions — an underappreciated seat-expansion vector.
insights.locator: Another thing my team does is live office hours for AI support

insights.claim: Deep AI vendor relationships are treated as strategic infrastructure — giving beta access ahead of general availability, a two-way channel to push product direction, and visibility into where the organization lags industry practice, with Cursor's team rules feature cited as a pain point solved through that channel.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: Design-partner status is a real, under-modelled advantage for early enterprise adopters, and a retention mechanism for AI tool vendors.
insights.locator: investing in your AI vendor relationships

insights.claim: Duolingo learned it was behind on evaluations by observing that its AI vendors were using evals internally, then copied the practice — vendor relationships functioning as a competitive-benchmarking channel.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: Evals are diffusing from AI labs into enterprise engineering practice via vendor contact, not literature — a leading indicator for eval tooling demand.
insights.locator: One example that I have for that is around evals

insights.claim: Duolingo's PR Risk Assessment buckets every code change as low, medium or high risk — or undetermined when the diff exceeds the token limit — and changes landing in the low-risk bucket that meet additional criteria are auto-approved by a bot and merged with no human reviewer.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: A working template for graduated autonomy: classify risk first, automate only the tail, keep an explicit undetermined bucket for cases the model cannot see.
insights.quote: What this means is that we allow you to merge your code without a human reviewer in these cases.
insights.locator: We have a system called the PR Risk Assessment

insights.claim: The risk-scoring pipeline runs like any other CI check — triggered on pull request push, it feeds the PR title, verification steps, the diff, a user prompt and a risk-bucketing prompt to an LLM and returns a risk tier plus an explanation that updates the CI check and bot approval status.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: Implementing AI governance as a CI check rather than a new surface is why adoption was frictionless — a reusable integration pattern.
insights.locator: How does our AI auto-approval bot work?

insights.claim: Meta pioneered this approach with its diff risk score, but used it in the opposite direction — gatekeeping high-risk changes to ship at safer times — and Duolingo pivoted to accelerating low-risk changes because adding friction was unacceptable in a ship-fast culture.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: The same risk-scoring primitive can be sold as a safety product or a velocity product; which framing wins depends entirely on the buyer's culture.
insights.quote: Duolingo is a company that likes to experiment and likes to ship fast, so adding friction was just not acceptable.
insights.locator: Participant 4: When you actually went through this journey

insights.claim: Duolingo's system is a scaled-back version of Meta's because its engineering org is 300 people rather than 300,000, but the speaker asserts the core principles remain the same — implying risk-scored autonomous review is viable well below hyperscaler scale.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: Lowers the size threshold at which AI code-review automation pays off, expanding the addressable market for such tooling into mid-size orgs.
insights.quote: Our system is a lot more scaled back because our engineering org is only 300 people and not 300,000 people.
insights.locator: I do want to call out, too, that Meta pioneered this work

insights.claim: The risk taxonomy is organization-specific in ways that resist generic productization: Duolingo classifies asset animations — such as the Duo character appearing at the end of a lesson — as wide-reaching changes, alongside universal categories like user permissions and infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: Off-the-shelf risk-scoring products will underperform without per-org tuning, favouring configurable platforms over fixed-rule vendors.
insights.locator: There's also a lot I have not included in here that is very Duolingo specific

insights.claim: Medium risk is defined by blast radius rather than diff size — API version mapping updates for the learning app and changes to foundational components like auth and logging are held back for two accountable humans even when the code change is small.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: Blast radius, not line count, is the right risk axis for automating review — a directly transferable rule for anyone building similar gating.
insights.quote: Updates to foundational components like auth, logging, things that have a larger blast radius even if the code change is small.
insights.locator: In terms of medium risk

insights.claim: Auto-approval is fenced by layered guardrails: repos can restrict it to code owners only, include or exclude specific directories, and it is disabled entirely for AWS resource changes, for repos with higher auditing requirements such as SOX or ISO covering the Duolingo English Test, and for new engineers during onboarding.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: Compliance scope (SOX/ISO) is the hard boundary on AI autonomy in engineering workflows — regulated surfaces stay human-reviewed regardless of model quality.
insights.locator: we have a ton of guardrails in place to mitigate risk

insights.claim: The code-owner restriction is largely psychological rather than statistical: about 80% of changes in a typical Duolingo repo already come from the 5 or 6 owners out of 20-30 contributors, so limiting auto-approval to owners is effectively the same population but provides a sense of security.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: Adoption of autonomous systems is bought with perceived control as much as actual risk reduction — a design lesson for anyone shipping agentic features.
insights.quote: Eighty percent of the code changes in that repo are already from the small group of people, so it is effectively the same, but it's just like a nice sense of security
insights.locator: locking down the auto approve bot to only code owner changes

insights.claim: Duolingo uses opt-in daily notification digests instead of per-PR review requests, drawing on the ship/show/ask framework so engineers retain visibility into what was merged without being interrupted every time.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: Batching visibility rather than eliminating it is how teams preserve oversight while removing synchronous review — an attention-budget design pattern.
insights.locator: Then a final guardrail is just around opt-in notifications per day

insights.claim: Misclassification reports arrive through a dedicated Slack channel at a few messages per week, get converted into an eval dataset pinning expected risk tiers and explanation keywords, and are used to fine-tune the risk prompt while staying backwards compatible with all prior reports.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: A cheap, human-sourced eval flywheel is the operating model for keeping prompt-based classifiers accurate — no labelling vendor required.
insights.quote: We take these reports and essentially put them in an eval list
insights.locator: The feedback loop portion of the PR risk scoring

insights.claim: AI literacy changed the nature of complaints: engineers moved from refusing to enable the auto-approve bot at all to actively wanting it on and reporting specific classification inaccuracies for fixing.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: The observable signal that an AI rollout has crossed the trust threshold is the shift from opt-out pressure to bug reports — a diagnostic for adoption maturity.
insights.quote: Now we see people are like, I really like having auto-approve on in my systems, but I just think there's an inaccuracy here that I want you to fix.
insights.locator: The feedback loop portion of the PR risk scoring

insights.claim: As the share of pull requests merged through the auto-approve bot climbed from roughly 0% to about 10% over six months, Duolingo's median time to merge across all PRs fell from about 18 hours to about 12 hours — a one-third reduction.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: The headline ROI number for autonomous code review: 10% of PRs automated produced a 33% cut in org-wide median merge latency.
insights.quote: we see that with that climb is the correlation of our median time to merge dropping from about 18 hours per pull request to about 12 hours per pull request
insights.locator: I also wanted to talk about the results of our auto approve bot system

insights.claim: The speaker argues the effect is non-linear: accelerating low-risk changes produces a cascading effect that speeds up medium- and high-risk merges too, because the 10% figure is measured against all PRs including those permanently ineligible for compliance or resource reasons.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: Queueing effects mean partial automation delivers more than its share of throughput gain — the ROI case is stronger than a linear model suggests.
insights.quote: when you accelerate the low-risk changes, there is that cascading effect that the median risk and the high-risk code changes also helps them
insights.locator: Some really exceptional things about this

insights.claim: Asked directly about defect rate, the speaker reports no discernible signal: of roughly 200 pull requests a day, maybe one or two are reverts of auto-approved changes, and it is hard to separate those from ordinary experimental reverts engineers make deliberately.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: The critical counterfactual — speed without quality loss — is supported but only weakly measured, which is the main diligence gap in the case study.
insights.quote: I think this project probably would have been shut down almost immediately if we had seen a significant defect rate like that.
insights.locator: Participant 3: You've showed very nicely the effect

insights.claim: The speaker states the auto-approve bot has to her knowledge never been involved in a site incident, and that it is conservative enough not to cause the churn and outages teams fear when enabling it.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: Absence of a headline incident after a year is the social proof that unblocks similar rollouts elsewhere — watch for the first public counterexample.
insights.quote: this, to my knowledge, has never been involved in like a side incident
insights.locator: Participant 1: I'm part of a team very similar in my company

insights.claim: The design was validated against existing behaviour rather than theory: research showed about 30% of Duolingo code changes were already being signed off with no comments at all, and those correlated well with the low-risk bucket, which is what justified scaling automation.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: Rubber-stamp rate is the measurable proxy for how much review is automatable in any org — a fast diligence test before building similar systems.
insights.quote: We have like 30% of our code changes with no feedback, so what's the point of pulling in people if they don't need to give feedback
insights.locator: One part of the research that I did to get the risk bucketing accurate

insights.claim: Auto-approval is optional and roughly 20-30% of eligible changes are still pushed to human review by their authors, mostly for the mentorship and feedback value rather than correctness.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: Voluntary opt-out at 20-30% puts a practical ceiling on automation rates and identifies mentorship, not verification, as the residual human function.
insights.locator: the other part of it is our auto-approval bot is optional

insights.claim: Asked how the value of 100% AI adoption is measured, the speaker concedes it is the golden unanswered question in the industry and offers only qualitative returns — engineers feeling empowered to build AI features into the product, and taking on more ambitious projects outside their subject-matter expertise.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: Even a sophisticated adopter cannot quantify the ROI of universal AI tool adoption — a caution against taking enterprise AI productivity claims at face value.
insights.quote: I think that is the golden question in industry right now overall
insights.locator: Participant 2: I think you mentioned that you're right now around 100% of developers

insights.claim: Deitke's scaling framework runs access, then experimentation via hackathons and shared learnings, then literacy through workshops, then observability through dashboards, then guardrails built with security, audit and legal, and only then autonomy and expansion.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: A sequenced maturity model that positions autonomous agents as the last step, not the first purchase — useful for judging where a given enterprise actually is.
insights.locator: Branching out in terms of like how to scale AI in your org

insights.claim: The observability dashboards double as a talent-scouting tool: spikes in an individual's AI usage prompt the team to nudge that person to share their techniques with the wider org.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: Usage telemetry as an internal-practice discovery mechanism is a non-obvious second use for AI observability spend.
insights.locator: Sometimes the tooling actually can help you say

insights.claim: The speaker's closing gate for anyone considering AI agents is a set of readiness questions — whether the organization built AI literacy and not just AI access, whether engineers feel empowered over the systems, and whether AI would feel empowering rather than imposed.
insights.speaker: Sarah Deitke
insights.so_what: Reframes AI agent deployment as a change-management prerequisite, predicting that orgs buying agents without enablement will see stalled adoption.
insights.quote: If AI is going to participate in your workflows, you need to empower your organization first.
insights.locator: Before you add AI agents and automate
